strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and clearly articulated gap between high-probability (HP) and mean-squared-error (MSE) convergence theory for decentralized SGD, situating the contribution clearly relative to a substantial body of prior centralized and decentralized literature.

Removes restrictive assumptions used in the closest prior work ([57]), namely uniformly bounded gradients and asymptotically vanishing noise, replacing them with standard heterogeneity/strong-convexity assumptions that match those used in MSE analyses.

Establishes linear speed-up in the number of users in the HP sense for both non-convex and strongly convex costs, which is a genuinely new result compared to all cited decentralized HP works, and is achieved via two technical contributions of independent interest: Lemma 2 (variance-reduction of decentralized noise in the HP/sub-Gaussian sense) and Lemma 5 (a sharper, more fine-grained MGF bound for 'almost decreasing' stochastic processes), the latter also improving on state-of-the-art centralized HP bounds.

Provides detailed, rigorous, and largely self-contained proofs in the appendix, including explicit derivation of transient times and direct, careful comparison with MSE-derived transient times, showing the HP rates match or strictly improve on them — a good tightness check.

Includes numerical experiments that validate both the exponential tail decay and the linear speed-up predictions, and are described with enough methodological detail (data generation, network construction, Monte Carlo estimation of tail probabilities) to be reproducible.

Includes an honest, non-trivial discussion of remaining limitations (dimension dependence, the necessity of assumption (A5), fixed vs. time-varying step-size trade-offs, extension to time-varying networks) rather than glossing over them.
weaknesses: The non-convex result still requires a (weaker but nontrivial) uniform heterogeneity bound (A5) rather than the average heterogeneity condition used in comparable MSE work (e.g., Koloskova et al.); the paper acknowledges this could likely be relaxed but does not do so, leaving a residual gap versus the tightest MSE assumptions.

The strongly convex analysis requires each local cost function fi to be strongly convex (not just the average f), and requires identical initialization across users for the cleanest form of Lemma 4/Theorem 2; both are stronger than what is needed in some MSE treatments (e.g., with gradient tracking), and the removal of these via GT/exact diffusion is left as future work.

The dimension dependence (√d for non-convex, d for strongly convex) is a real limitation relative to prior MSE and even some HP bounds cited in the paper; the proposed fix (norm-sub-Gaussian noise) is only sketched and not incorporated into the main results.

Novelty of the base algorithm is limited — the paper analyzes a standard variant of vanilla DSGD without gradient tracking or other bias-correction mechanisms, so the results, while technically deep, are incremental in terms of algorithmic contribution; the extensions to more practical GT-based methods are deferred entirely to future work.

The extension to directed/time-varying networks (Appendix J) is only sketched at a high level (via an existing contraction lemma from [57]) rather than fully worked out with matching guarantees, so the practical scope of the results is somewhat narrower than claimed in the abstract's generality.

Numerical experiments, while illustrative, are conducted only on synthetic quadratic (strongly convex) objectives with Gaussian noise and moderate network sizes; no experiments on non-convex objectives (e.g., neural networks) or heavier-tailed but still sub-Gaussian noise are provided to stress-test the theory in more realistic settings.

strengths: Clearly identifies and closes a genuine gap in the literature: existing high-probability (HP) results for Decentralized SGD (e.g., Lu et al. [57]) require uniformly bounded gradients and/or asymptotically vanishing noise, assumptions that are much stronger than those needed for MSE convergence; this paper shows HP convergence under the same (weaker) assumptions as MSE analyses.

First work (to the authors' knowledge) to establish a linear speed-up in the number of users for DSGD in the high-probability sense, for both non-convex and strongly convex costs, matching or even improving (strongly convex case) transient times compared to MSE-derived rates.

Introduces genuinely useful technical machinery beyond incremental adaptation of prior proofs: Lemma 2 shows a variance-reduction effect of decentralized averaging in the sub-Gaussian/HP sense; Lemma 4 gives an MGF bound on the consensus gap without requiring bounded heterogeneity; Lemma 5 gives a sharper MGF bound for 'almost decreasing' stochastic processes that is stated (plausibly) to be of independent interest even in centralized SGD analysis.

The paper provides a careful, explicit, and honest comparison against the closest prior work [57], explaining precisely why that work cannot achieve linear speed-up even under its own assumptions (no variance-reduction result, and step-size choice), which strengthens the credibility of the claimed improvements.

Extensive appendix with full proofs, an explicit derivation of transient times, a dedicated discussion of why/where the sqrt(d) or d dimension dependence arises and how it might be mitigated, and a discussion of extension to (directed) time-varying networks.

Numerical experiments, while simple, are designed thoughtfully to probe exactly the two claimed phenomena (exponential tail decay and linear speed-up with n), and the results appear consistent with the theory.
weaknesses: The final rates carry an extra dependence on problem dimension (√d for non-convex, d for strongly convex) that is absent in prior MSE bounds and in [57]'s HP bound; while the authors discuss this candidly (Appendix K) and suggest a norm-sub-Gaussian noise assumption could reduce it to log(d), this is not established as a formal result in the paper, leaving a real (flagged but unresolved) weakness.

For strongly convex costs, the analysis still requires each local cost fi (not just the global average) to be strongly convex, which is noted as stronger than what gradient-tracking (GT)-based methods require; heterogeneity assumption (A5) for non-convex costs is also stated to be slightly stronger than the average-heterogeneity condition used in comparable MSE analyses (e.g., Koloskova et al.), and the authors only conjecture it can be relaxed rather than proving it.

Numerical validation is restricted to a synthetic quadratic (strongly convex) objective with Gaussian noise; there is no experiment on non-convex or realistic ML workloads (e.g., neural networks), which limits confidence that the theoretical predictions (particularly for the non-convex results, which are a primary contribution) translate to more practical settings.

The core algorithm (vanilla DSGD, Adapt-Then-Combine) and overall proof strategy (MGF-based bounding, offset trick, unrolling consensus recursions) build heavily on established techniques from centralized HP SGD analysis and decentralized MSE analysis; the contribution is best characterized as a careful/technical tightening and generalization of known frameworks rather than a conceptually new algorithmic or analytical paradigm.

The strongly convex last-iterate result requires identical initialization across users for the tightest bound; while the authors note this can be relaxed at the cost of an extra term, this again is not fully worked out.

Practical significance is somewhat narrow: the paper explicitly leaves extension to PL costs, gradient-tracking/bias-correction methods (which would remove the heterogeneity and per-node strong-convexity assumptions), and heavy-tailed noise to future work, meaning several of the most practically relevant generalizations are unaddressed within the paper itself.

strengths: Closes an important and clearly articulated gap between high-probability (HP) and mean-squared-error (MSE) convergence theory for Decentralized SGD, showing for the first time that DSGD converges in HP under the same cost assumptions as needed for MSE convergence (removing uniformly bounded gradients and vanishing noise conditions required by the closest prior work [57]).

Establishes the first linear speed-up result for decentralized SGD in the HP sense, for both non-convex and strongly convex costs, and shows transient times that match or strictly improve upon those implied by existing MSE analyses (e.g., strictly sharper transient time for strongly convex costs than Alghunaim & Yuan's MSE bound).

Introduces several technical results of independent interest beyond the specific DSGD application: (i) Lemma 2, showing the variance-reduction effect of decentralized averaging carries over to the HP/sub-Gaussian setting; (ii) Lemma 4, a sharp MGF bound on the consensus gap for strongly convex costs that avoids heterogeneity assumptions; (iii) Lemma 5, a refined MGF bound for 'almost decreasing' stochastic processes that is tighter than existing centralized HP bounds (e.g., [31,32,40]) and could be reused in other analyses.

The paper is unusually careful and transparent about its own limitations, including an explicit discussion of the unavoidable dimension dependence (√d and d factors) and how it could be mitigated under stronger noise assumptions (Appendix K), as well as a detailed comparison to the closest related works with concrete technical explanations of why prior approaches cannot achieve linear speed-up (Appendix I).

Provides thorough proof sketches in the main text and complete, well-organized proofs in the appendix, along with a discussion of extensions to time-varying/directed networks (Appendix J), increasing confidence in correctness and reproducibility of the theoretical claims.

Numerical experiments, while synthetic, directly test the two central theoretical claims (exponential tail decay and linear speed-up in the number of users) and are designed with reasonable control for confounds (fixed network connectivity, fixed heterogeneity across different n).
weaknesses: Bounds carry a √d (non-convex) or d (strongly convex) dependence on problem dimension that is not present in comparable MSE or prior HP bounds for DSGD; although the authors discuss mitigations, this remains a real limitation for high-dimensional problems such as deep networks.

The strongly convex analysis (Lemma 4) requires identical initialization across all users (x_i^1 = x_j^1); while the authors state this can be relaxed at the cost of an additional geometrically decaying term, this relaxation is not carried through the main theorem.

Assumption (A5) (worst-case, rather than average, heterogeneity bound) is slightly stronger than what is used in some MSE-based comparisons (e.g., Koloskova et al.), and the paper only conjectures, without proof, that this can be relaxed via techniques from that work.

The scope is restricted to light-tailed (sub-Gaussian) noise and static (or, via appendix discussion, time-varying but still undirected/strongly-connected) networks; extensions to heavy-tailed noise and gradient-tracking-based bias-corrected methods (to remove strong convexity/heterogeneity assumptions) are left as future work, somewhat narrowing the immediate applicability.

Experiments are limited to a synthetic quadratic/strongly-convex setting with Gaussian noise; there is no empirical validation on non-convex objectives (e.g., neural network training) despite non-convex theory being a central contribution of the paper.

The presentation is extremely dense with heavy notational overhead, and the core intuition behind why the 'offset trick' and the MGF-balancing arguments work is somewhat compressed in the main text, requiring significant appendix cross-referencing to fully verify claims.

strengths: Closes a well-motivated and clearly articulated gap between HP and MSE convergence theory for decentralized SGD, removing restrictive assumptions (uniformly bounded gradients, asymptotically vanishing noise) used in the closest prior work [58].
First result establishing linear speed-up in the number of users for DSGD in the high-probability sense, matching a well-known feature of decentralized MSE guarantees.

Technically substantial contribution: Lemma 2 establishes variance-reduction of decentralized averaging in the HP/MGF sense; Lemma 4 gives a tight MGF bound on the consensus gap without bounded heterogeneity for strongly convex costs; Lemma 5 provides a sharper MGF recursion bound for 'almost decreasing' processes that is of independent interest even for centralized SGD.

Sharp transient-time analysis: matches the non-convex MSE-implied transient time and is provably better (strictly sharper) than the MSE-implied transient time for strongly convex costs, which is a nice consistency/tightness check.

Extensive, careful proofs are provided in the appendix (technical lemmas, martingale concentration arguments, explicit derivations of Sk, Dk constants, transient-time derivations), aiding reproducibility.

Honest and detailed discussion of limitations, including the mild log(d) dependence introduced by working with sub-Gaussian random vectors, with justification of why this arises and comparison to alternative definitions of sub-Gaussianity.
Thorough, well-organized comparison to prior decentralized HP works (especially [58]) and centralized HP works, clarifying exactly where the technical novelty lies.

Numerical experiments, though synthetic, are designed thoughtfully to isolate and verify the two key theoretical claims (exponential tail decay and linear speed-up), with controlled network/heterogeneity settings across different n.
weaknesses: Numerical validation is limited to a synthetic strongly convex quadratic setting; no experiments on non-convex/neural network training or real datasets are provided, which limits demonstration of practical significance despite the theoretical scope covering non-convex costs.

Strong convexity is required to hold for each individual local cost fi (not just the global average), which is a common but still restrictive assumption; heterogeneity bound (A5) is also slightly stronger (max instead of average heterogeneity) than some existing MSE analyses, acknowledged by the authors but not resolved.

Theorem 2's clean form relies on identical initialization across users (x_i^1 = x_j^1); while the authors state this can be relaxed at the cost of extra geometrically decaying terms, this weakens the immediate generality of the main strongly-convex result.

The scope is restricted to vanilla DSGD under light-tailed noise; extensions to heavy-tailed noise, gradient-tracking-based bias-correction methods, or general (non-strongly-convex, e.g., PL) costs are left to future work, somewhat narrowing the immediate applicability of the results.
The paper carries an unresolved mild log(d) dimension dependence not present in comparable MSE results or in [58]'s bounds, which is flagged as an open question rather than resolved.

The presentation is very dense with heavy notation and many constants/conditions on step-size and t0, which, combined with the highly technical appendix, may hinder accessibility and independent verification by non-specialist readers.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and well-motivated gap in the literature: existing high-probability (HP) results for Decentralized SGD require uniformly bounded gradients or vanishing noise, which is inconsistent with the assumptions needed for MSE-type results and with the centralized HP literature.
Removes these restrictive assumptions for both non-convex and strongly convex costs, replacing them with standard heterogeneity/strong-convexity conditions used in MSE analyses.

Establishes, for the first time, a linear speed-up in the number of users for DSGD in the HP sense, matching (and in the strongly convex case, strictly improving) the transient times implied by corresponding MSE bounds.

Several technical lemmas (variance-reduction of averaged noise in the HP/MGF sense - Lemma 2; MGF bound on the consensus gap without bounded heterogeneity - Lemma 4; sharp MGF control of 'almost decreasing' processes - Lemma 5) are nontrivial and plausibly of independent interest, including for centralized analyses.

The paper is unusually careful and transparent in comparing its assumptions, rates, and transient times against the closest related work ([58]) and against MSE counterparts, and explicitly discusses the origin and necessity of a mild log(d) dependence rather than hiding it.

Proofs are provided in detail in the appendix, and the paper includes a derivation of transient times and a discussion of how linear speed-up is technically obtained (Appendix J), which aids reproducibility and understanding of where the technical difficulty lies.
weaknesses: The experimental validation is very limited: a single synthetic strongly-convex quadratic problem with Gaussian noise, small dimension/network sizes, and no deep-learning or non-convex empirical validation despite non-convex theory being a main contribution; this weakens confidence that the theoretical predictions (exponential tails, linear speed-up) generalize beyond a toy quadratic setting.

The strongly convex results still require every local cost fi to be individually strongly convex (A6) and the non-convex results still require a heterogeneity bound (A5) that is strictly stronger than the average-heterogeneity condition used in comparable MSE works (e.g., [11]); the paper acknowledges this gap but does not close it, leaving the improvement over prior work only partial.

The scope is narrower than the main point of comparison [58] in one respect: [58] handles the more general PL condition, whereas this paper only treats non-convex and strongly convex costs, deferring PL costs to future work.

The results are restricted to light-tailed (sub-Gaussian) noise and vanilla DSGD without bias-correction mechanisms like gradient tracking, which the paper itself notes would be needed to remove the heterogeneity/strong-convexity-of-each-fi assumptions; this limits the practical applicability of the stated 'relaxed assumptions' claim.

The step-size conditions and final rates involve a very large number of problem-dependent constants and nested min/max expressions (see Theorems 1 and 2), which, while common in this literature, substantially reduces interpretability and makes it hard to assess tightness or practical usability of the bounds without extensive unpacking.

The core proof strategy (bounding MGFs of descent-type inequalities, consensus gap, and using offset tricks) is a fairly direct, if careful, combination of existing centralized HP techniques ([31,32,33,40]) with existing decentralized MSE techniques ([11,20,25]); the novelty is more in careful technical execution than in a fundamentally new algorithmic or conceptual idea, which may limit the paper's broader significance.

The static network assumption is the default setting, with time-varying extension relegated to an appendix sketch rather than a fully worked result, somewhat overstating the generality claimed in the main text.

strengths: Addresses a clearly articulated and well-motivated gap: closing the discrepancy between assumptions needed for HP vs. MSE convergence of decentralized SGD, removing restrictive uniformly-bounded-gradient and vanishing-noise assumptions used in prior work (e.g., [58]).

Provides multiple technical contributions of apparent independent interest: Lemma 2 establishing variance-reduction of decentralized averaging in the HP (MGF) sense, Lemma 4 bounding the MGF of the consensus gap without bounded heterogeneity for strongly convex costs, and Lemma 5 giving a sharper MGF bound for 'almost decreasing' stochastic processes that improves on existing centralized HP proof techniques.

First decentralized SGD HP convergence result with linear speed-up in the number of users, matching or improving transient times derived from MSE-based literature; the paper carefully derives and discusses these transient times (Appendix I).
Thorough and explicit comparison with the closest related work [58], clearly delineating what assumptions are removed and why their approach could not achieve linear speed-up.

Extensive, apparently rigorous appendix with full proofs, including discussion of edge cases (unknown time horizon, time-varying networks, dimension dependence, Polyak-Ruppert averaging) that strengthens confidence in correctness and completeness.

Numerical experiments, although synthetic, are designed thoughtfully to isolate and verify the two central theoretical claims (exponential tail decay and linear speed-up), with controlled heterogeneity/connectivity across comparisons.
weaknesses: Experiments are limited to simple synthetic quadratic (strongly convex) problems; despite motivating the work with large-scale/LLM training scenarios, there is no empirical evaluation on realistic non-convex deep learning tasks, leaving the practical relevance of the theoretical gains less validated.

The non-convex result still relies on a (weaker, but still restrictive) bounded-heterogeneity assumption (A5) with per-user (not average) heterogeneity bound; the paper acknowledges this could likely be relaxed following [11] but does not do so, leaving a gap between the strongest known MSE assumptions and this work's non-convex assumptions.

The strongly-convex analysis requires strong convexity of every local cost fi (not just the global average) and same initialization across users for the cleanest bound (extensions are only sketched, not fully worked out in the main results).

A mild but unresolved log(d) dimension dependence is introduced (absent from both compared MSE results and prior HP work [58]); while discussed, it is not fully resolved and could matter in high-dimensional settings.

Promised extensions (PL costs, gradient-tracking/exact-diffusion to remove heterogeneity assumptions, heavy-tailed noise) are left as future work, so the practical scope of the removed assumptions is narrower than the discussion might suggest.

Given the heavy technical machinery and length of proofs, independent verification by reviewers within normal review timeframes is difficult, which is a practical reproducibility/review-burden concern even if the derivations appear internally consistent.
